title: Joining Tables
description: Connect related tables with primary/foreign keys, INNER and OUTER joins, self joins, UNION, and multi-table joins

lessons.title: Keys & Relationships
lessons.description: Understand primary keys and foreign keys — the glue that connects tables together

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a primary key and a foreign key are, and how they let two tables relate to each other.

sections.title: 🔑 Primary keys: each row's unique ID
sections.content:
A **primary key** is a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table — no two rows can share one, and it can't be NULL. In our schema, `customer_id` is the primary key of `customers`, `order_id` is the primary key of `orders`, and so on.

Think of it like a social security number or a serial number: it exists purely so you can point at *this one specific row* and no other.

sections.title: 🔗 Foreign keys: pointing to another table's row
sections.content:
A **foreign key** is a column that stores another table's primary key value, creating a link between the two tables. In `orders`, the `customer_id` column is a foreign key — it doesn't identify the order itself, it points at *which customer* placed it.

```sql
orders.customer_id  →  points to  →  customers.customer_id
orders.order_id  = primary key of orders (unique per order)
```

This is exactly the relationship that lets you ask questions that span two tables, like "which customer placed order #482?" — and it's what the JOIN keyword (next lesson) is built around.

sections.title: 🧭 One-to-many, the most common relationship
sections.content: Most relationships in our schema are **one-to-many**: one customer can have many orders, but each order belongs to exactly one customer. You can always spot the "many" side — it's the table holding the foreign key (`orders.customer_id`), because each of its rows points to just one row on the "one" side (`customers.customer_id`).

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing which side of a relationship is "one" and which is "many" — the foreign key always lives on the many side. Assuming a foreign key column has the same name as the primary key it points to — it usually does in tidy schemas, but not always.

questions.question: What makes a primary key different from other columns?
options: It must always be text
It uniquely identifies each row and can't be NULL or duplicated
It's always the first column in the table
It automatically sorts the table
questions.explanation: A primary key's whole job is to uniquely identify a row — every value must be unique, and it can never be NULL.

questions.question: What is orders.customer_id an example of?
options: A primary key of the orders table
A foreign key pointing to customers.customer_id
A calculated column
An index name
questions.explanation: It's a foreign key: it stores a value from another table's primary key (customers.customer_id) to link an order back to the customer who placed it.

questions.question: In a one-to-many relationship between customers and orders, which table holds the foreign key?
options: customers, because it's the 'one' side
orders, because it's the 'many' side and each order points to one customer
Both tables need the same foreign key
Neither — foreign keys are only used in many-to-many relationships
questions.explanation: The 'many' side (orders, since one customer can have many orders) holds the foreign key pointing back to the 'one' side (customers).

questions.question: Can a table have more than one candidate key, even though it has only one primary key?
options: Yes, other unique columns can serve as candidate keys even if not chosen as the primary key
No, a table can only ever have exactly one unique column
No, only foreign keys can be unique
Yes, but only in tables with fewer than 10 rows
questions.explanation: A table can have several columns that could each uniquely identify a row; only one is designated the primary key.

questions.question: What does a foreign key reference?
options: A primary key in another (or the same) table
A column with no constraints at all
The table's row count
A column that must contain NULLs
questions.explanation: A foreign key points to a primary key elsewhere, establishing the relationship between tables.

questions.question: Why must a primary key be unique?
options: So each row can be unambiguously identified
So the table can be sorted faster
Because SQL requires all columns to be unique
Because foreign keys are otherwise disabled
questions.explanation: Uniqueness is what allows a primary key to reliably identify exactly one row.

questions.question: Can a primary key contain a NULL value?
options: No, a primary key column cannot contain NULLs
Yes, as long as it's still unique among non-NULL values
Only in the first row of a table
Only if the table has no foreign keys
questions.explanation: Primary keys must be both unique and non-NULL to reliably identify every row.

questions.question: What kind of relationship exists between customers and orders when one customer can place many orders?
options: A one-to-many relationship
A many-to-many relationship
A one-to-one relationship
No relationship at all
questions.explanation: One customer linked to many orders is the classic one-to-many relationship, with the foreign key living on the 'many' side.

lessons.title: INNER JOIN
lessons.description: Combine rows from two tables based on a matching key

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write an INNER JOIN to combine two related tables and understand exactly which rows it keeps.

sections.title: 🧩 Combining two tables
sections.content:
A `JOIN` lets a query pull columns from more than one table at once, matched up by their key relationship:

```sql
SELECT orders.order_id, customers.name, orders.total_amount
FROM orders
INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;
```

The `ON` clause is the crucial part — it tells the database **how** the two tables relate. Without it, the database wouldn't know which customer goes with which order.

sections.title: ✅ INNER JOIN keeps only matches
sections.content:
`INNER JOIN` (often just written `JOIN`) returns only the rows where the matching condition is true on **both sides**. If an order somehow had no matching customer, that order would simply be left out of the result.

That's the defining feature to remember: **INNER JOIN = only rows that match in both tables.** The next lesson covers what to do when you want unmatched rows kept too.

sections.title: 🏷️ Table aliases keep it readable
sections.content:
Typing full table names gets tedious, especially with more joins. Give tables short aliases instead:

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.total_amount
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
```

`o` and `c` now stand in for the table names everywhere else in the query — this becomes essential once you're joining three or four tables.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the ON clause — most databases require it, and without it you can accidentally create a cross join (every row paired with every row). Joining on the wrong pair of columns, which silently produces a table that looks plausible but is wrong.

questions.question: What does the ON clause in a JOIN specify?
options: Which columns to display in the output
How the two tables relate — the condition used to match their rows
The order results should be sorted in
Which table to filter first
questions.explanation: ON defines the matching condition between the two tables — typically a foreign key column equaling the primary key it points to.

questions.question: If an order has a customer_id that doesn't exist in the customers table, what happens with INNER JOIN?
options: The order still appears, with NULLs for customer columns
The order is excluded from the result entirely
The query throws an error
The customer_id is automatically corrected
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN only keeps rows where the join condition matches on both sides. An order with no matching customer row simply doesn't appear in the result.

questions.question: In FROM orders AS o INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id, what is o?
options: A new column
An alias standing in for the orders table for the rest of the query
A function
A typo for 'order'
questions.explanation: AS o creates a short alias for the orders table, so it can be referred to as o instead of the full table name in the rest of the query.

questions.question: What rows does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Only rows that have matching values in both joined tables
Every row from the left table, matched or not
Every row from both tables regardless of match
Only rows with NULL foreign keys
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN only keeps rows where the join condition finds a match in both tables.

questions.question: Can you JOIN more than two tables in one query?
options: Yes, by chaining multiple JOIN clauses together
No, SQL only supports joining exactly two tables
Only if the tables are named identically
Only using a subquery, never a direct JOIN
questions.explanation: Multiple JOIN clauses can be chained to combine data from several tables in one query.

questions.question: What is a common reason to use a table alias like `AS o` in a JOIN?
options: To keep the query shorter and more readable when referencing columns
Because JOIN requires aliases to function at all
To permanently rename the table in the database
To prevent the join from matching any rows
questions.explanation: Aliases are a readability convenience, letting you write o.customer_id instead of orders.customer_id repeatedly.

questions.question: What happens to unmatched rows from either table in an INNER JOIN?
options: They are excluded from the result entirely
They appear with NULLs filling in for the missing side
They cause the query to fail
They are automatically merged with the nearest matching row
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN strictly requires a match on both sides — no match means the row doesn't appear at all.

questions.question: Does the order of tables in an INNER JOIN change the result set (ignoring column order)?
options: No, INNER JOIN is symmetric, so the matched rows are the same either way
Yes, joining A to B gives different matched rows than B to A
Only if one of the tables has no primary key
Only when more than two tables are involved
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN's matching logic is symmetric — the same rows match regardless of which table is listed first.

lessons.title: OUTER JOINs
lessons.description: Keep unmatched rows too, with LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER JOIN

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain when to use LEFT JOIN instead of INNER JOIN, and read the NULLs it produces for unmatched rows.

sections.title: 👈 LEFT JOIN: keep everything on the left
sections.content:
`LEFT JOIN` keeps **every row from the left (first) table**, whether or not it has a match on the right. Where there's no match, the right table's columns just come back as `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.total_amount
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

This is exactly how you'd answer "show me every customer, including ones who have never ordered anything" — an INNER JOIN would silently drop those customers, but LEFT JOIN keeps them with NULL order columns.

sections.title: 🔎 Finding the unmatched rows on purpose
sections.content:
A very common pattern combines `LEFT JOIN` with a `WHERE ... IS NULL` check to find rows with *no* match at all:

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
```

This answers "which customers have never placed an order?" — a question INNER JOIN literally cannot answer, because it only ever shows matches.

sections.title: ↔️ RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN
sections.content:
`RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image of LEFT JOIN — it keeps every row from the **right** table instead. In practice, most people just swap the table order and use LEFT JOIN, so RIGHT JOIN is rarely written.

`FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps **everything from both sides**, matched where possible and NULL-padded where not. It's less common day-to-day, but useful for spotting mismatches between two tables that are supposed to line up.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using INNER JOIN when the real question is about *missing* relationships — the customers-with-no-orders example above is a classic case where only LEFT JOIN gives the right answer. Forgetting that after a LEFT JOIN, columns from the right table can be NULL, and code that doesn't expect that will break.

questions.question: What's the key difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
options: They always return the same result
INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows; LEFT JOIN also keeps unmatched left-table rows, with NULLs on the right
LEFT JOIN is faster but less accurate
INNER JOIN can only be used with two tables, LEFT JOIN with three or more
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN drops rows with no match on either side. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless, filling in NULL for right-table columns when there's no match.

questions.question: How would you find customers who have never placed an order?
options: INNER JOIN customers to orders and filter WHERE order_id IS NULL
LEFT JOIN customers to orders and filter WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
RIGHT JOIN orders to customers with no filter
This can't be done with joins
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every customer even with no matching order (NULL in order columns), and the WHERE o.order_id IS NULL filter then isolates exactly the customers with no match.

questions.question: What does FULL OUTER JOIN return?
options: Only rows that match in both tables
Only rows from the left table
Every row from both tables, matched where possible and NULL-padded where not
An error, since it isn't valid SQL
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN combines the behavior of LEFT and RIGHT JOIN: it keeps everything from both tables, matching where it can and filling NULLs where it can't.

questions.question: What does a LEFT JOIN guarantee about the left (first-listed) table's rows?
options: Every row from the left table appears in the result, matched or not
Only matched rows from the left table appear
The left table's rows are dropped if no match exists
The left table must have a primary key to be used
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN always keeps every row from the left table, filling in NULLs for the right side if there's no match.

questions.question: When a LEFT JOIN finds no match on the right table, what appears in the right table's columns?
options: NULL values
Zero (0)
An empty string
The row is simply omitted
questions.explanation: Unmatched right-side columns are filled with NULL rather than being omitted or defaulted to another value.

questions.question: What's a practical use case for a LEFT JOIN with a NULL check?
options: Finding customers who have never placed an order
Finding customers who have placed at least one order
Sorting customers alphabetically
Counting the total number of products
questions.explanation: Filtering for NULL on the joined side after a LEFT JOIN reveals rows from the left table with no match — like customers with zero orders.

questions.question: Is RIGHT JOIN the mirror image of LEFT JOIN?
options: Yes, RIGHT JOIN keeps every row from the right table instead of the left
No, RIGHT JOIN behaves identically to INNER JOIN
No, RIGHT JOIN is not a valid SQL keyword
Yes, but only for numeric columns
questions.explanation: RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT JOIN, guaranteeing all rows from the right-hand table instead.

questions.question: Why is FULL OUTER JOIN sometimes described as combining LEFT and RIGHT JOIN?
options: Because it keeps unmatched rows from both tables, not just one side
Because it only returns matched rows from both sides
Because it requires exactly two matching columns
Because it always returns an empty result
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both the left and right tables simultaneously.

lessons.title: Self Joins & UNION
lessons.description: Join a table to itself, and stack two result sets together

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a self join to compare rows within one table, and use UNION to combine two queries' results.

sections.title: 🪞 Self joins: a table joined to itself
sections.content:
Sometimes the relationship you need is *within* one table — like employees having a manager who is also an employee. A **self join** joins a table to itself, using two different aliases to tell the two 'copies' apart:

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
```

`e` represents each employee, and `m` represents that employee's manager — same table, two roles. LEFT JOIN is used here so employees with no manager (like the CEO) still show up, with NULL in the manager column.

sections.title: ➕ UNION: stacking two result sets
sections.content:
`UNION` combines the rows from two separate `SELECT` queries into one result, stacked on top of each other — as long as both queries return the **same number of columns with compatible types**.

```sql
SELECT name, 'customer' AS role FROM customers
UNION
SELECT name, 'employee' AS role FROM employees;
```

This is useful when you want a single combined list from two different tables that represent similar things.

sections.title: 🔁 UNION vs UNION ALL
sections.content:
Plain `UNION` automatically removes duplicate rows across the two result sets — which means it does extra work to check for duplicates. `UNION ALL` keeps every row from both queries, duplicates included, and is faster since it skips that check.

Use `UNION ALL` whenever you know there won't be duplicates, or you don't care about them — it's the better default for performance.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting that both queries in a UNION need matching column counts and compatible types. Reaching for a self join when a simple filter would do — self joins are for genuinely comparing rows within the same table, like employee-to-manager.

questions.question: In a self join like FROM employees AS e LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id, what are e and m?
options: Two different physical tables
Two aliases for the same employees table, representing different roles in the comparison
Built-in SQL keywords
Column names
questions.explanation: e and m are just two aliases pointing at the same employees table, letting the query treat each row twice — once as 'the employee' and once as 'the manager'.

questions.question: What's required for two SELECT queries to be combined with UNION?
options: They must query the same table
They must return the same number of columns with compatible types
They must both use GROUP BY
Nothing — any two queries can be combined
questions.explanation: UNION stacks result sets row-by-row, so the two queries need the same number of columns, in a compatible order and type, for the combination to make sense.

questions.question: What's the main practical difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION ALL is only for numeric columns
UNION removes duplicate rows across both result sets; UNION ALL keeps every row, including duplicates, and is faster
UNION can only combine two queries; UNION ALL can combine more
There is no difference
questions.explanation: UNION does extra work to de-duplicate the combined rows. UNION ALL skips that check and keeps everything, which is both simpler in meaning and cheaper to run.

questions.question: What is a self join used for?
options: Comparing rows within the same table to each other, like an employee to their manager
Joining a table to itself twice with no purpose
Joining a table only to itself and no other table
A join that always returns zero rows
questions.explanation: A self join relates rows in a table to other rows in that same table, common for hierarchical data like employee/manager.

questions.question: What must be true about the columns selected in each part of a UNION?
options: Each SELECT must return the same number of columns with compatible types
The column names must be identical across both queries
Each query must come from the exact same table
UNION requires exactly one column in each query
questions.explanation: UNION requires matching column count and compatible types, though column names can differ.

questions.question: What does UNION do with exact duplicate rows across the combined result?
options: Removes duplicates automatically, keeping only distinct rows
Keeps every duplicate row
Causes an error if duplicates exist
Randomly drops half of the duplicate rows
questions.explanation: Plain UNION deduplicates the combined result; UNION ALL keeps every row including duplicates.

questions.question: When would UNION ALL be preferred over UNION?
options: When you want to keep duplicates, or know there won't be any and want better performance
Never — UNION ALL is always worse
Only when combining more than three queries
Only when working with text columns
questions.explanation: UNION ALL skips the deduplication step, which is both simpler when duplicates aren't a concern and generally faster.

questions.question: In a self join aliasing a table as `e` and `m`, what does the join condition typically compare?
options: A foreign key column on one alias to the primary key on the other, like e.manager_id = m.employee_id
Two completely unrelated columns
The table name to itself as a string
Nothing — self joins require no ON condition
questions.explanation: The join condition links each employee's manager_id to another row's employee_id within the same table.

lessons.title: Multi-Table Joins in Practice
lessons.description: Chain three or more joins together to answer a real, multi-table question

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Chain multiple JOINs across three or more tables to answer a question that no single table can answer alone.

sections.title: 🧵 Chaining joins
sections.content:
Real questions often span more than two tables. "What did each customer actually buy?" needs `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, and `products` all connected:

```sql
SELECT c.name, p.name AS product, oi.quantity, oi.unit_price
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o       ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products AS p     ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;
```

Each `JOIN` adds one more table into the mix, following the chain of foreign keys: customer → order → order item → product.

sections.title: 🧠 Reading a multi-join query
sections.content:
When a query has several joins, read it as a chain of connections rather than all at once:

• Start at `FROM` — that's your anchor table
• Each `JOIN ... ON ...` adds one more table, connected by a key
• By the time you reach `SELECT`, you can picture one wide, combined table made from all of them

It also helps to build these queries incrementally: start with two tables, run it, confirm it looks right, then add the next join.

sections.title: 💰 Joining with an aggregate: revenue per product
sections.content:
Joins and GROUP BY combine naturally. "Which products earned the most revenue?" needs a join (to get product names) plus an aggregate (to total the revenue):

```sql
SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN products AS p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Joining tables that aren't actually related by a key, which silently multiplies rows in strange ways. Losing track of which alias refers to which table once there are four or five of them — pick short, memorable aliases and stay consistent.

questions.question: To find out what products each customer bought, which tables need to be joined together (based on our schema)?
options: Only customers and products
customers, orders, order_items, and products, following the foreign key chain
Only orders and order_items
Just products, since it lists all items
questions.explanation: The chain of foreign keys runs customer → order → order item → product, so all four tables need to be joined to connect a customer to the specific products they bought.

questions.question: What's a good strategy for writing a query with four or five joins?
options: Write the whole thing at once and hope it's correct
Build it incrementally — start with two tables, verify, then add joins one at a time
Avoid using aliases to keep it simple
Always use RIGHT JOIN for every table
questions.explanation: Building incrementally — join two tables, check the result, then add the next join — makes it much easier to catch mistakes early instead of debugging a large query all at once.

questions.question: In SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue, what is being calculated per row before the SUM?
options: Just the unit_price
The line-item total: quantity times unit price for that order item
The customer's total spend
The number of products in the category
questions.explanation: quantity * unit_price computes the revenue for one order line item; SUM then adds those line totals together per group (here, per product).

questions.question: Why might a query need to join four or five tables together?
options: Because the information needed spans data that's spread across several related tables
Because SQL requires at least four tables in every query
Because JOIN only works with an even number of tables
Because more joins always make a query faster
questions.explanation: Real business questions often require combining data scattered across several normalized tables.

questions.question: What's a reasonable strategy for building a complex multi-join query?
options: Build and test it one join at a time, verifying results at each step
Write every join at once with no testing
Avoid using aliases entirely to keep it simple
Always join every table in the database regardless of need
questions.explanation: Incrementally adding and verifying each join makes it much easier to catch mistakes before the query grows complex.

questions.question: What happens to a computed expression like `quantity * unit_price` when wrapped inside SUM()?
options: It's calculated per row first, then those per-row values are summed together
It's summed first, then multiplied once at the end
It causes a SQL syntax error
It only works if quantity and unit_price are in the same table
questions.explanation: The multiplication happens per row before the aggregate SUM combines all those row-level results.

questions.question: Why is it useful to alias computed columns like `SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue`?
options: It gives a clear, reusable name to reference the calculated value elsewhere in the query
It changes the underlying calculation
It's required for the multiplication to execute
It converts the column into a primary key
questions.explanation: Aliasing a computed expression makes the result readable and lets you reference it in ORDER BY or elsewhere.

questions.question: When joining multiple tables, why does column naming sometimes need a table prefix like `o.customer_id`?
options: To disambiguate when the same column name exists in more than one joined table
Because SQL requires every column reference to include a prefix
Because prefixes make queries run faster
Because unprefixed columns are always interpreted as strings
questions.explanation: A prefix resolves ambiguity when multiple joined tables share a column name, like customer_id appearing in both customers and orders.
